originalSource.title: CelesTrak General Perturbations (GP) and Supplemental GP (SupGP) element sets
originalSource.version: Live service; no snapshot retained in this repository

processing: Tracker fetches two documents at runtime, in the reader's own browser, and commits neither: the ISS supplemental ephemeris, which is derived from NASA's published trajectory, and whichever Starlink post-deployment stack vector CelesTrak is currently listing. Both are cached for two hours, which is the publisher's own stated update cadence.

SupGP is preferred over GP wherever it exists, because it is derived from the operator's own data. GP is the fallback for the ISS and is recorded as such on the page, so a prediction can always say which of the two it came from.

The usage policy asks machine-to-machine consumers to stop querying on any non-200 response rather than retrying. The query is configured with no retries and the deployment fetch stops at the first refusal; a failure produces no pass rather than more requests.

No element set is committed to this repository. The fixtures in the unit tests and in scripts/verify/tracker-refinement.mjs are Orbit Studio's own constructed elements — the shape of a station and of a deployment stack — because no authoritative grant was found for redistributing CelesTrak's own data.

rights.attribution: Orbital element sets from CelesTrak (Dr. T.S. Kelso); the ISS ephemeris is derived from NASA's published trajectory and a Starlink stack vector from SpaceX's published state vector.

processing: The verified v1.0.0 package preserves the immutable 2026-06-27 GCAT satcat snapshot, its exact original checksum, normalized 69,703-record products, SQLite query database, 1957-2026 annual presence, reconstruction candidates, quality ledger, schemas, build scripts, and package checksums.

scripts/build-satellite-web-catalog.py verifies the package first, queries only the canonical SQLite database, and deterministically exports all 69,620 Earth-associated payload, rocket-body, component, and debris rows into src/data/generated/satelliteCatalog.web.json.

The web export preserves GCAT JCAT and available SATCAT identities, classification, owner/status, lifecycle bounds, source perigee, source apogee, source inclination, source orbit epoch, and package reconstruction angles.

For historical rows without package-precomputed angles, the export applies the package-prescribed SHA-256 algorithm keyed by the stable JCAT identifier. Runtime code never creates a second hash or random reconstruction authority.

Twenty-one latest members and 244 all-history rows with insufficient or physically invalid orbital envelopes remain catalog-only. Displayed reconstructed states are not observed, live, current, or exact positions.

originalSource.publisher: Mallama, A., Cole, R. E., Respler, J., Harrington, S., Lee, R. and Worley, A. (2024)

processing: The fields used are the ones the granule actually carries, confirmed by inspecting a live file rather than by reading documentation: ACM, a four-level mask whose flag_meanings read 'clear probably_clear probably_cloudy cloudy'; Cloud_Probabilities, a uint16 with scale_factor 1.5261e-05 giving the probability that the pixel is cloudy; and DQF, whose flag_meanings distinguish good, bad, space and degraded quality. Pixels the product calls unusable are reported as no observation rather than as clear sky.

A reading for a place is always the native pixel covering it, at the product's own two-kilometre resolution. Map requests may skip pixels by stride when the view holds more of them than can be drawn, and the stride falls to one as the reader zooms in; a stride skips pixels and never averages them, so every value shown is one NOAA published.

Nothing is interpolated between categories. A classification has nothing between its levels, and a value invented between two of them would be a measurement nobody made. Rendering may be smoothed; the evidence is not.
The probability is presented as a per-pixel confidence and never as a sky-cover fraction. The two are different quantities and Tracker does not convert one into the other.

A small Netlify function stands between the browser and the service. NOAA's own object storage sets permissive CORS but distributes HDF5, which would mean shipping an HDF5 reader to every reader; the THREDDS server subsets the same product over DAP4 into a few kilobytes but sends no CORS headers. The function asks for exactly the pixels requested, decodes the DAP4 chunk stream, and returns the values unaltered. It resamples nothing.

Every grid constant — the sub-satellite longitude, the ellipsoid, the scan-angle offsets and steps, the scene size — is read from the granule being used, because the two spacecraft differ and the grid has been redefined before.

originalSource.title: Open-Meteo Air Quality API (Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service)
originalSource.publisher: Open-Meteo, serving Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service model output
originalSource.version: Runtime API, not a pinned snapshot; hourly aerosol_optical_depth and pm2_5, requested with past_days=1 and forecast_days=3

processing: Fetched from the browser at the observer’s selected location, coordinates rounded to two decimal places so observers in one model cell share a cache entry and a precise location is never used as a cache key. One past day is requested alongside three forecast days because the NowCast below needs the twelve hours preceding the instant being asked about; without it the series begins at 00:00 UTC of the current day and no twelve-hour window exists before noon.

Aerosol optical depth at 550 nm is the value the interface reasons from; it is converted to magnitudes of extinction (1.0857 per unit optical depth) rather than shown as a bare index, because magnitudes are the unit the observing judgement is made in. The conversion is the definition of optical depth, not a calibration.

Surface PM2.5 is used for one purpose only: a health reading. It is NOT converted directly to an AQI. The US AQI's PM2.5 breakpoints are defined against a 24-hour average, so an index is derived only from an EPA NowCast — the twelve hourly values ending at the instant in question, weighted by w^i where w = max(0.5, 1 - (max-min)/max) over the available values, summed and divided by the same weights, truncated to one decimal place. EPA's validity rule is applied unchanged: at least two of the three most recent hours must be present, and where it is not met no index is computed and none is displayed. Missing hours are dropped from both sums and are never forward-filled. The AQI category thresholds are a separate function that takes the NowCast concentration as its only input. Where no NowCast is available the interface may still report the hourly concentration as a concentration in µg/m³, without an index and without any AQI category name, since those names belong to a scale that has not been evaluated.

Aerosol optical depth is merged into the weather snapshots by timestamp with a 45-minute tolerance; a snapshot with no aerosol sample within tolerance keeps its nulls and renders as unmeasured rather than as clean air. The PM2.5 series is read separately and in full, because a NowCast cannot be computed from a single merged snapshot value.
Requested as a separate query from the weather providers so that losing it costs one condition card rather than the whole row.

Aerosol optical depth and surface PM2.5 are never combined into a single figure. Where no aerosol model covers a location the interface shows no transparency card rather than substituting the ground-level particulate reading for it.

Both quantities are modelled output from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service, not monitor observations, and hours after the present are forecasts. The interface distinguishes a NowCast whose window has already elapsed from one that projects forward, and states which on the card.

originalSource.version: Runtime API, not a pinned snapshot; ovation_aurora_latest.json, noaa-planetary-k-index-forecast.json, planetary_k_index_1m.json

processing: Tracker's second runtime external request, and the only one that is not per-location: NOAA publishes one global grid, so the request carries no coordinates and every observer shares one fetch. Nothing about the observer is transmitted.

The OVATION grid is parsed into a typed array indexed by whole degrees. NOAA’s published quantity — the probability of visible aurora in percent — is carried through unmodified and is attributed to NOAA wherever it is shown. Tracker applies no model of its own on top of it.

Three horizons are kept apart rather than merged: the OVATION nowcast (valid roughly half an hour), the three-day planetary K-index forecast, and nothing at all beyond that. The interface refuses to speak past the third.
The nowcast and the K-index are separate queries so that a dropped request for one retries without discarding the other. Neither response is stored; both are held in memory for the session only.

Freshness is read from the product’s own forecast time rather than from a chosen interval: a grid past its forecast time is ageing, and past a further grace period is stale. A stale grid stops producing a probability, an outlook and a ranking weight entirely, and what NOAA last reported is carried separately so the interface can show it as history rather than as advice.

The ranking weight Tracker derives from NOAA’s probability is an editorial transformation and is declared as one in code (auroraRankingStrength returns editorial: true with a stated basis). NOAA publishes a probability of visible aurora; it does not publish an opinion about whether that beats Saturn.

Whether aurora could be seen from a location, as distinct from being overhead at it, is derived by Tracker rather than read from NOAA. OVATION reports the probability of aurora overhead; emission occurs at altitude, so it clears the horizon from far outside the oval. SWPC publishes exactly this as the aurora viewline, but only as rendered rasters under /experimental/images/aurora_dashboard/ — there is no coordinate form in /json/, /experimental/json/ or /products/ — so it is not consumed. Instead the horizon reach is computed as R*arccos(R/(R+h)) and the apparent elevation by spherical geometry, with h taken from NOAA's published range of 80-500 km (100 km for the bright lower border, 400 km for tall red emission). The resulting angle and direction are Tracker's derivation and are never attributed to NOAA.

Copy pass: the sentences Tracker builds from this data were rewritten for plainness without changing what they claim. Nowcast-versus-forecast wording, the expiry language, the attribution of NOAA's probability and the disclaimer that the derived horizon angle is Tracker's own are all preserved verbatim in meaning.

originalSource.title: Earth Observation Group Annual VIIRS Nighttime Lights V2.1, annual average, 2024, 15 arc-second
originalSource.publisher: Earth Observation Group, Payne Institute for Public Policy, Colorado School of Mines (data); obtained through the OpenLandMap redistribution on Zenodo (T. Hengl), record 17294744
originalSource.originalSha256: md5:0b976892d40c2d0d99177c727289eaf2 (Zenodo-published checksum, verified on download; 63,713,625 bytes)

processing: Obtained from the Zenodo redistribution rather than from EOG directly, because eogdata.mines.edu now requires an account: every path under it, including direct file URLs, 302-redirects to a Keycloak sign-in. The Zenodo record is CC BY 4.0 and states that its 2012-2024 layers are the Annual VNL V2 images of Elvidge et al. (2021); only its pre-2012 layers are extrapolated, and none of those are used here. Swapping in EOG's own average_masked GeoTIFF is a one-argument change to the build script for anyone who holds an account.
The source is EPSG:4326 at 15 arc-seconds, 86400x35849, int16, holding radiance in nW/cm2/sr multiplied by ten. Verified on download against the publisher's own md5.

scripts/build-light-pollution-tiles.py resamples it into Web Mercator XYZ tiles, 256px, zoom 0 to 8, and writes them as one sparse archive with a JSON index. Zoom 8 is 611m per pixel at the equator and about 430m at 45 degrees, which is where the source's own grid lands; storing finer tiles would store interpolation rather than data.

Each output pixel is the mean of the source pixels inside it, computed from a summed-area table. Nearest-neighbour was the first implementation and was replaced: the two grids never align, so it returned whichever neighbour was closest to the output centre, which across a city gradient is a real error - central Portland measures 9.7 nW and its neighbour 14.4, and nearest-neighbour returned the neighbour.

Tiles are 8-bit RGB PNGs with the value split across red (high byte) and green (low byte). 16-bit greyscale is 8% smaller and was tried first, but a browser cannot read one back: decoding needs a 2D canvas and a canvas is 8 bits per channel, so a 16-bit PNG is silently truncated. This is the same reason Terrarium elevation tiles encode the way they do.

Only tiles containing light exist - 14,928 of them, 47.8 MB. A missing tile means no artificial light was detected anywhere in it, which is true of most of the planet: 2.6% of the source's valid pixels carry any light at all. The browser reads single tiles by HTTP range request, so a reader fetches the 400 KB index once and then a handful of tiles, not the archive.

The value is carried as radiance all the way to the interface and quoted there alongside its band. It is NOT presented as a Bortle class, an SQM reading, or a limiting magnitude, and no claim is made about which objects will be visible: those are statements about the sky, and deriving them from upward radiance needs an atmospheric scattering model that Tracker does not have. The bands are fixed thresholds on a log scale - 0.25, 1, 4, 16 and 64 nW/cm2/sr - documented in lightPollution.ts and chosen as round numbers before checking where any particular town fell.

Replaces a 2048x966 render of NASA's Black Marble, about 14 km per pixel, which could not resolve a city: Bend, Oregon, population 100,000, registered as unlit and was reported to the reader as dark. Validated after the change at central Portland 12.3, Wood Village 3.4, Bend 2.9, Sisters 0.8, Manhattan 47.7 and London 14.4 nW/cm2/sr, with the Alvord Desert and the Atacama at zero. Each of those figures was confirmed against the source raster's own pixels before tiling, so the differences are in the measurement and not in the rendering.

originalSource.title: MapLibre GL JS, an open-source WebGL renderer for vector map tiles

The library's tile-decoding worker is bundled by Vite and its address handed to MapLibre with setWorkerUrl. Left to resolve itself the worker looks for a sibling file that a hashed asset directory does not contain, and every failure that follows is silent: the style loads, no error is raised, and no tile is ever drawn.
The renderer's own hostname appears in the bundle only inside the library's licence banner and error strings. Tracker makes no request to maplibre.org at runtime.

Repeated world copies are on, because the Pacific is one place and a map that stops at the antimeridian makes the reader drag back around to see the other half. Everything Tracker draws over the geography is emitted into the copies either side as well, so a repeated world is never lit where the real one is dark, and a click on any copy is wrapped back to the one longitude that names that place.

originalSource.title: Photon geocoder over OpenStreetMap data
originalSource.version: Runtime API, not a pinned snapshot; queried per search

processing: Place search runs from the browser against a public Photon instance. Queries are the text the reader typed; no identifier accompanies them and nothing is stored.
Requests are debounced so a free service is not asked for a result per keystroke, and searches shorter than three characters are not sent at all.

Results are re-ranked locally to favour the categories an observer means — campsites, parks, reserves, summits, viewpoints and trailheads above street addresses — because the campground case is the one the location contract exists for.
A coordinate pair typed into the same field is parsed locally and never sent anywhere, which is the fallback for a site too remote to be in any database.
The adapter declares its cost as public-no-fee and the router will not return a cost-bearing geocoder on the free path, enforced the same way as for weather.

originalSource.title: Mapterhorn public terrain tiles, Terrarium-encoded elevation built from 148 open elevation datasets
originalSource.publisher: Mapterhorn (tile build and service); the 148 national, regional and agency producers listed at mapterhorn.com/attribution (data)
originalSource.version: Runtime tile service, not a pinned snapshot; TileJSON read per session, tiles fetched on demand

processing: Terrain tiles are fetched from the public Mapterhorn instance at runtime, as 512px Terrarium-encoded WebP. Requests carry a tile coordinate and nothing that identifies the reader. No API key is used and no account exists.

The tiles are read twice, for different purposes. The map draws them as a MapLibre hillshade layer for relief. Separately, Tracker decodes them off-screen to elevations and computes a horizon profile along the bearing of the event a reader has opened: elevation = (R*256 + G + B/256) - 32768 metres, then apparent angle tan(a) = (h - d^2/2R) / d against a refracted Earth radius of 7/6 R.

The analytical read is capped at zoom 11 and 40 km, and at zoom 10 and 18 km for an event's own track. Not for cartographic reasons: the service throttles, and a measured 21-way concurrent fetch returned 11 tiles, 8 timeouts and 2 aborts inside 20 seconds. Four concurrent requests with a 20-second budget completes in about 2 seconds.

Sampling stops at Mapterhorn's zoom 15, which is where the service stops serving distinct data. Asking for more returns an overzoomed tile with the same posts resampled, which would manufacture precision the terrain does not have.

The horizon result is reported in half-degree steps and can return 'unknown'. The underlying post spacing varies by more than two orders of magnitude across the 148 sources — 0.5 m in parts of France, 30 m where only Copernicus GLO-30 covers — so a single stated accuracy for the layer would be false anywhere but the source it was measured on.
This dependency is a courtesy public endpoint on the same terms as the basemap, and is recorded as such in terrainSource.ts.

Verified against ground truth at four sites: Kansas plains 544 m with a 0-0.1 degree horizon; Portland 21 m with West Hills at 4.2 degrees west; Chamonix 1035 m, matching the town's published elevation exactly, with valley walls at 22.4 degrees east and 20.4 degrees west; Sahara 544 m at 1-2 degrees.

Nothing in the catalogue is non-commercial, share-alike or research-only, so drawing and redistributing derived map images is not in question. Most of those licences do require attribution and no map corner can carry 148 credits; the publisher's own mechanism, which those licences accept, is a link to the full list, and Tracker's attribution control renders that link. What is unresolved is the same thing that is unresolved for the basemap and for place search: production reliance on a free public endpoint with no usage agreement, on a service that is measurably rate-limited.

originalSource.title: MET Norway Locationforecast 2.0 and the US National Weather Service API
originalSource.publisher: Norwegian Meteorological Institute; NOAA National Weather Service
originalSource.version: Runtime API, not a pinned snapshot; queried live per observing location

processing: This is Tracker's first runtime external request. Forecasts are fetched from the browser at the observer's selected location and are never bundled, stored on a server, or attributed to a user.

Requests are keyed and cached by forecast grid cell, coordinates rounded to two decimal places, rather than by user. Rounding is both a caching requirement of the providers and a deliberate limit on the precision of the location that is transmitted.

Routing prefers the National Weather Service inside the United States for its finer grid and falls back to MET Norway globally. Both are declared public-no-fee; the router will not return a cost-bearing adapter on the free path.

Provider schemas are normalised into one internal ConditionSnapshot. MET Norway's fog area fraction is converted to a nominal visibility in metres, which is the only place a provider's value is reinterpreted rather than renamed.
No smoke or air-quality source is fetched. Those snapshot fields stay null, and the model treats null as unknown rather than as clean air.

rights.licenseOrBasis: MET Norway Locationforecast is published under CC BY 4.0 and the National Weather Service API is US Government work in the public domain, so redistribution of the *data* is not in question. What is unresolved is compliance with the providers' identification requirement: both ask a caller to send a User-Agent identifying the application, and a browser cannot — User-Agent is a forbidden header name in the Fetch standard, so the browser discards it and sends its own. Verified empirically against an echo service. Resolving this means routing through a caching proxy that can set the header, which is a server and therefore a running cost.
